'''Paul D. Seymour''' {{post-nominals|size=100|FRS}} (born 1950) is a British [[mathematician]] known for his work in [[discrete mathematics]], especially [[graph theory]]. He (with others) was responsible for important progress on [[regular matroid]]s and [[totally unimodular matrix|totally unimodular matrices]], the [[four colour theorem]], [[linkless embedding]]s, [[Robertson–Seymour theorem|graph minors and structure]], the [[perfect graph]] conjecture, the [[Hadwiger conjecture (graph theory)|Hadwiger conjecture]], [[claw-free graph]]s, [[χ-bounded]]ness, and the [[Erdős–Hajnal conjecture]]. Many of his recent papers are available from his website.<ref name="Papers website">{{cite web|last=Seymour|first=Paul|title=Online Papers|url=https://web.math.princeton.edu/~pds/online.html|access-date=26 April 2013}}</ref>

Seymour is currently the [[Albert Baldwin Dod]] Professor of [[Mathematics]] at [[Princeton University]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://dof.princeton.edu/about/faculty/professorships|title=Professorships &#124; Dean of the Faculty}}</ref> He won a [[Sloan Fellowship]] in 1983, and the [[Ostrowski Prize]] in 2003;<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Allyn Jackson |title=Seymour Receives Ostrowski Prize |journal=Notices of the AMS |volume=51 |page=900 |url=https://www.ostrowski.ch/pdf/Seymour.pdf}}</ref> and (sometimes with others) won the [[Fulkerson Prize]] in 1979, 1994, 2006 and 2009, and the [[George Pólya Prize|Pólya Prize]] in 1983 and 2004. He received an honorary doctorate from the [[University of Waterloo]] in 2008, one from the [[Technical University of Denmark]] in 2013, and one from the [[École normale supérieure de Lyon]] in 2022. He was an invited speaker in the 1986 [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] and a plenary speaker in the 1994 [[International Congress of Mathematicians]]. He became a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]] in 2022.<ref name="FRS2022">{{cite web|title=Outstanding scientists elected as Fellows and Foreign Members of the Royal Society
|url=https://royalsociety.org/news/2022/05/new-fellows-2022/|access-date=11 May 2022}}</ref>

==Early life==
Seymour was born in [[Plymouth]], England in 1950.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Biographies |url=https://opentext.uleth.ca/Combinatorics/section-66.html#Seymour |access-date=2025-09-07 |website=opentext.uleth.ca |language=en-US}}</ref> Seymour was a student at [[Plymouth College]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.plymouthcollege.com/information/about-plymouth-college|work=About Plymouth College|title=Plymouth College Alumni Leaders and Champions|access-date=2025-03-07}}</ref> and then studied at [[Exeter College, Oxford]], gaining a [[Bachelor of Arts|BA]] degree in 1971,  [[Master of Science|MS]] degree  in 1972, and [[Doctor of Philosophy|D.Phil]] and [[Master of Arts|MA]] in 1975.<ref name="Seymour-cv"/> His doctoral dissertation, ''Matroids, Hypergraphs and the Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem'', was supervised by [[Aubrey William Ingleton]].<ref>{{mathgenealogy|50728}}</ref>

==Career==
From 1974 to 1976 he was a college research fellow at [[Swansea University|University College of Swansea]]. Then he returned to Oxford for 1976–1980 as a Junior Research Fellow at [[Merton College, Oxford]], with the year 1978–79 at [[University of Waterloo]].<ref name="Seymour-cv">{{cite web|title=Paul Seymour's CV
|url=https://web.math.princeton.edu/~pds/papers/vita/vita.pdf|access-date=27 May 2022}}</ref> He became an associate and then a full professor at [[Ohio State University]], [[Columbus, Ohio]], between 1980 and 1983, where he began research with [[Neil Robertson (mathematician)|Neil Robertson]],
a fruitful collaboration that continued for many years. From 1983 until 1996, he was a senior scientist at [[Bellcore]] (Bell Communications Research), [[Morristown, New Jersey]] (now [[Telcordia Technologies]]). He was also an adjunct professor at [[Rutgers University]] from 1984 to 1987 and at the University of Waterloo from 1988 to 1993. He became professor at [[Princeton University]] in 1996.<ref name="Seymour-cv">{{cite web|title=Paul Seymour's CV
|url=https://web.math.princeton.edu/~pds/papers/vita/vita.pdf|access-date=27 May 2022}}</ref> At Princeton he was given the Albert Baldwin Dod Professorship in 2016.<ref name=":0" />

He is Editor-in-Chief (jointly with [[Carsten Thomassen (mathematician)|Carsten Thomassen]]) for the ''[[Journal of Graph Theory]]'',<ref name="JGT-board">{{cite web|title=Journal of Graph Theory Editorial Board
|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/page/journal/10970118/homepage/editorialboard.html|doi=<!-- 10.1002/(ISSN)1097-0118 removed, does not go to editorial board subpage --> |access-date=27 May 2022}}</ref> and an editor for ''[[Combinatorica]]''<ref name="Combinatorica-board">{{cite web|title=Combinatorica Editorial Board
|url=https://www.springer.com/journal/493/editors|access-date=27 May 2022}}</ref> and the ''[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory|Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B]]''.<ref name="JCTB-board">{{cite web|title=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B Editorial Board
|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/journal-of-combinatorial-theory-series-b/about/editorial-board|access-date=27 May 2022}}</ref>

[[File:PaulSeymour2010.jpg|thumb|Seymour giving a talk in 2010]]

==Personal life==
Seymour's brother [[Leonard W. Seymour]] is Professor of [[gene therapy]] at [[Oxford University]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/health/6251303.stm|title=Cold virus to aid cancer patients|date=11 January 2007}}</ref> In 1979, Seymour got married and had two children.<ref name=":0" />

==Major contributions==
Combinatorics in Oxford in the 1970s was dominated by [[matroid theory]], due to the influence of [[Dominic Welsh]] and [[Aubrey William Ingleton]]. Much of Seymour's early work, up to about 1980, was on matroid theory, and included three important matroid results: his D.Phil. thesis on matroids with the max-flow min-cut property<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Seymour |first1=P.D. |title=The matroids with the max-flow min-cut property |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B]] |date=1977 |volume=23 |issue=2–3 |pages=189–222 |doi=10.1016/0095-8956(77)90031-4|doi-access=free }}</ref> (for which he won his first Fulkerson prize); a characterisation by excluded minors of the matroids representable over the three-element field;<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Seymour, P.D. |title=The matroids representable over <math>{\rm GF}(3)</math> |journal=Problèmes combinatoires et théorie des graphes (Colloq. Internat. CNRS, Univ. Orsay, Orsay, 1976) |date=1978 |volume=260 |pages=381–383 |series=Colloq. Internat. CNRS}}</ref> and a theorem that all [[regular matroid]]s consist of graphic and cographic matroids, and a special matroid called ''R''<sub>10</sub>, pieced together in a simple way<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Seymour |first1=P.D. |title=Decomposition of regular matroids |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B]] |date=1980 |volume=28 |issue=3 |pages=305–359 |doi=10.1016/0095-8956(80)90075-1|doi-access= }}</ref> (which won his first [[George Pólya Prize|Pólya prize]]). There were several other significant papers from this period: a paper with Welsh on the critical probabilities for bond percolation on the square lattice;<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Seymour |first1=P.D. |author2-link=Dominic Welsh |last2=Welsh, D.J.A. |title=Percolation Probabilities on the Square Lattice |journal=Annals of Discrete Mathematics |date=1978 |volume=3 |pages=227–245 |doi=10.1016/S0167-5060(08)70509-0|isbn=9780720408430 }}</ref> a paper on edge-multicolouring of cubic graphs,<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Seymour |first1=P.D. |title=On multi-colourings of cubic graphs, and conjectures of Fulkerson and Tutte |journal=[[Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society]] |date=1979 |volume=3 |issue=3 |pages=423–460 |doi=10.1112/plms/s3-38.3.423}}</ref> which foreshadows the matching lattice theorem of [[László Lovász]]; a paper proving that all bridgeless graphs admit nowhere-zero 6-flows,<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Seymour, P.D. |title=Nowhere-zero 6-flows| journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B]] |date=1981| volume=30| issue=2|pages=130–135|doi=10.1016/0095-8956(81)90058-7|doi-access=free}}</ref> a step towards [[nowhere-zero flow|Tutte's nowhere-zero 5-flow conjecture]]; and a paper solving the two-paths problem (also introducing the [[cycle double cover]] conjecture),<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Seymour |first1=P.D. |title=Disjoint paths in graphs |journal=[[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]] |date=1980 |volume=29 |issue=3 |pages=293–309 |doi=10.1016/0012-365X(80)90158-2|doi-access= }}</ref> which was the engine behind much of Seymour's future work.

In 1980 he moved to Ohio State University, and began work with Neil Robertson. This led eventually to Seymour's most important accomplishment, the so-called "Graph Minors Project", a series of 23 papers (joint with Robertson), published over the next thirty years, with several significant results:
the [[graph structure theorem|graph minors structure theorem]], that for any fixed graph, all graphs that do not contain it as a minor can be built from graphs that are essentially of bounded genus by piecing them together at small cutsets in a tree structure;<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Robertson, N. |last2=Seymour |first2=P. |title=Graph minors. XVII. Taming a vortex |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B]] |date=1999 |volume=77 |issue=1 |pages=162–210 |doi=10.1006/jctb.1999.1919|author1-link= Neil Robertson (mathematician)|doi-access=free }}</ref>
a proof of a conjecture of [[Klaus Wagner|Wagner]] that in any infinite set of graphs, one of them is a minor of another (and consequently that any property of graphs that can be characterised by excluded minors can be characterised by a finite list of excluded minors);<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Robertson, N. |last2=Seymour |first2=P. |title=Graph minors. XX. Wagner's conjecture |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B]] |date=2004 |volume=92 |issue=2 |pages=325–357 |doi=10.1016/j.jctb.2004.08.001|author1-link= Neil Robertson (mathematician)|doi-access=free }}</ref>
a proof of a similar conjecture of [[Crispin Nash-Williams|Nash-Williams]] that in any infinite set of graphs, one of them can be immersed in another;<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Robertson, N. |last2=Seymour |first2=P. |title=Graph minors XXIII. Nash-Williams' immersion conjecture |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B]] |date=2010 |volume=100 |issue=2 |pages=181–205 |doi=10.1016/j.jctb.2009.07.003|author1-link= Neil Robertson (mathematician)|doi-access=free |citeseerx=10.1.1.304.8831 }}</ref>
and polynomial-time algorithms to test if a graph contains a fixed graph as a minor, and to solve the k vertex-disjoint paths problem for all fixed k.<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Robertson, N. |last2=Seymour |first2=P. |title=Graph minors. XIII. The disjoint paths problem |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B]] |date=1995 |volume=63 |issue=1 |pages=65–110 |doi=10.1006/jctb.1995.1006|author1-link= Neil Robertson (mathematician)|doi-access=free }}</ref>

In about 1990 [[Robin Thomas (mathematician)|Robin Thomas]] began to work with Robertson and Seymour. Their collaboration resulted in several important joint papers over the next ten years:
a proof of a conjecture of [[Horst Sachs|Sachs]], characterising by excluded minors the graphs that admit [[linkless embedding]]s in 3-space;<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Robertson, N. |last2=Seymour, P. |last3=Thomas, R. |title=Sachs' linkless embedding conjecture |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B]] |date=1995 |volume=64 |issue=2 |pages=185–227 |doi=10.1006/jctb.1995.1032|author1-link=Neil Robertson (mathematician) |author2-link=Paul Seymour (mathematician) |author3-link=Robin Thomas (mathematician) |doi-access=free }}</ref>
a proof that every graph that is not five-colourable has a six-vertex complete graph as a minor (the four-colour theorem is assumed to obtain this result, which is a case of [[Hadwiger conjecture (graph theory)|Hadwiger's conjecture]]);<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Robertson, N. |last2=Seymour, P. |last3=Thomas, R. |title=Hadwiger's conjecture for <math>K_6</math>-free graphs |journal=[[Combinatorica]] |date=1993 |volume=13 |issue=3 |pages=279–361 |doi=10.1007/BF01202354|s2cid=9608738 |author1-link=Neil Robertson (mathematician) |author3-link=Robin Thomas (mathematician) }}</ref>
with [[Daniel P. Sanders|Dan Sanders]], a new, simplified, computer based proof of the [[four color theorem|four-colour theorem]];<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Robertson, N. |last2=Sanders, D. |last3=Seymour, P. |last4=Thomas, R. |title=The four-colour theorem |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B]] |date=1997 |volume=70 |issue=1 |pages=2–44 |doi=10.1006/jctb.1997.1750|author1-link=Neil Robertson (mathematician) |author2-link=Daniel P. Sanders |author4-link=Robin Thomas (mathematician) |doi-access=free }}</ref>
and a description of the bipartite graphs that admit [[Pfaffian orientation]]s.<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Robertson, N. |last2=Seymour, P. |last3=Thomas, R. |title=Permanents, Pfaffian orientations, and even directed circuits |journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |date=1999 |volume=150 |issue=3 |pages=929–975 |doi=10.2307/121059|jstor=121059 |arxiv=math/9911268 |s2cid=7489315 |author1-link=Neil Robertson (mathematician) |author3-link=Robin Thomas (mathematician) }}</ref>
In the same period, Seymour and Thomas also published several significant results: (with [[Noga Alon]]) a separator theorem for graphs with an excluded minor,<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Alon, N. |last2=Seymour, P. |last3=Thomas, R. |title=A separator theorem for nonplanar graphs |journal=[[Journal of the American Mathematical Society]] |date=1990 |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=801–808 |jstor=1990903 |author1-link=Noga Alon |author3-link=Robin Thomas (mathematician) |doi=10.2307/1990903 |doi-access=free }}</ref> extending the [[planar separator theorem]] of [[Richard Lipton]] and [[Robert Tarjan]]; a paper characterizing [[treewidth]] in terms of [[Bramble (graph theory)|brambles]];<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Seymour, P. |last2=Thomas, R. |title=Graph searching and a min-max theorem for tree-width |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B]] |date=1993 |volume=58 |issue=1 |pages=22–33 |doi=10.1006/jctb.1993.1027|author2-link=Robin Thomas (mathematician) |doi-access=free }}</ref> and a polynomial-time algorithm to compute the [[Branch-decomposition|branch-width]] of planar graphs.<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Seymour, P. |last2=Thomas, R. |title=Call routing and the ratcatcher |journal=[[Combinatorica]] |date=1994 |volume=14 |issue=2 |pages=217–241 |doi=10.1007/BF01215352|s2cid=7508434 |author2-link=Robin Thomas (mathematician) }}</ref>

In 2000, Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas were supported by the [[American Institute of Mathematics]] to work on the [[perfect graph|strong perfect graph conjecture]], a famous open question that had been raised by [[Claude Berge]] in the early 1960s. Seymour's student [[Maria Chudnovsky]] joined them in 2001, and in 2002 the four jointly proved the conjecture.<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Chudnovsky, M. |last2=Robertson, N. |last3=Seymour, P. |last4=Thomas, R. |title=The strong perfect graph theorem |journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |date=2006 |volume=164 |issue=1 |pages=51–229 |doi=10.4007/annals.2006.164.51|s2cid=119151552 |author1-link=Maria Chudnovsky |author2-link=Neil Robertson (mathematician) |author4-link=Robin Thomas (mathematician) |doi-access=free |arxiv=math/0212070 }}</ref> Seymour continued to work with Chudnovsky, and obtained several more results about induced subgraphs, in particular (with [[Gérard Cornuéjols|Cornuéjols]], Liu, and [[Kristina Vušković|Vušković]]) a polynomial-time algorithm to test whether a graph is perfect,<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Chudnovsky, M. |last2=Cornuéjols, G |last3=Liu, X. |last4=Seymour, P. |last5=Vus̆ković, K. |title=Recognizing Berge graphs |journal=[[Combinatorica]] |date=2005 |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=143–186 |doi=10.1007/s00493-005-0012-8|s2cid=2229369 |author1-link=Maria Chudnovsky |author2-link=Gérard Cornuéjols |author5-link=Kristina Vušković }}</ref> and a general description of all claw-free graphs.<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Chudnovsky, M. |last2=Seymour, P. |title=Claw-free graphs. V. Global structure |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B]] |date=2008 |volume=98 |issue=6 |pages=1373–1410 |doi=10.1016/j.jctb.2008.03.002|author1-link=Maria Chudnovsky |doi-access=free |citeseerx=10.1.1.125.1835 }}</ref> Other important results in this period include: (with Seymour's student [[Oum Sang-il|Sang-il Oum]]) [[parameterized complexity|fixed-parameter tractable]] algorithms to approximate the [[clique-width]] of graphs (within an exponential bound) and the branch-width of matroids (within a linear bound);<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Oum, S. |last2=Seymour, P. |title=Approximating clique-width and branch-width |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B]] |date=2006 |volume=96 |issue=4 |pages=514–528 |doi=10.1016/j.jctb.2005.10.006|author1-link=Oum Sang-il |doi-access=free |citeseerx=10.1.1.139.9829 }}</ref> and (with Chudnovsky) a proof that the roots of the independence polynomial of every claw-free graph are real.<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Chudnovsky, M. |last2=Seymour, P. |title=The roots of the independence polynomial of a clawfree graph |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B]] |date=2007 |volume=97 |issue=3 |pages=350–357 |doi=10.1016/j.jctb.2006.06.001|author1-link=Maria Chudnovsky |doi-access=free |citeseerx=10.1.1.118.3609 }}</ref>

In the 2010s, Seymour worked mainly on [[χ-bounded]]ness and the [[Erdős–Hajnal conjecture]]. In a series of papers with Alex Scott and partly with Chudnovsky, they proved two conjectures of [[András Gyárfás]], that every graph with bounded clique number and sufficiently large chromatic number has an induced cycle of odd length at least five,<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Scott, A. |last2=Seymour, P. |title=Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. I. Odd holes |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B]] |date=2016 |volume=121 |pages=68–86 |doi=10.1016/j.jctb.2015.10.002|s2cid=52874586 |doi-access=free |arxiv=1410.4118 }}</ref> and has an induced cycle of length at least any specified number.<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Chudnovsky, M. |last2=Scott, A. |last3=Seymour, P. |title=Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. III. Long holes |journal=[[Combinatorica]] |date=2017 |volume=37 |issue=6 |pages=1057–1072 |doi=10.1007/s00493-016-3467-x|arxiv=1506.02232 |s2cid=2560430 |author1-link=Maria Chudnovsky }}</ref> The series culminated in a paper of Scott and Seymour proving that for every fixed k, every graph with sufficiently large chromatic number contains either a large complete subgraph or induced cycles of all lengths modulo k,<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Scott, A. |last2=Seymour, P. |title=Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. X. Holes with specific residue |journal=[[Combinatorica]] |date=2019 |volume=39 |issue=5 |pages=1105–1132 |doi=10.1007/s00493-019-3804-y|arxiv=1705.04609 |s2cid=51746725 }}</ref> which leads to the resolutions of two conjectures of [[Gil Kalai]] and Roy Meshulam connecting the chromatic number of a graph with the [[Homology (mathematics)|homology]] of its [[independence complex]]. There was also a polynomial-time algorithm (with Chudnovsky, Scott, and Chudnovsky and Seymour's student Sophie Spirkl) to test whether a graph contains an induced cycle with length more than three and odd.<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Chudnovsky, M. |last2=Scott, A. |last3=Seymour, P. |last4=Spirkl, S. |title=Detecting an odd hole |journal=[[Journal of the ACM]] |date=2020 |volume=67 |issue=1 |page=12pp |doi=10.1145/3375720|s2cid=119705201 |author1-link=Maria Chudnovsky |doi-access=free |hdl=10012/18527 |hdl-access=free |arxiv=1903.00208 }}</ref> Most recently, the four jointly resolved the 5-cycle case of the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture, which says that every graph without an induced copy of the 5-cycle contains an independent set or a clique of polynomial size.<ref group=pub>{{cite journal |last1=Chudnovsky, M. |last2=Scott, A. |last3=Seymour, P. |last4=Spirkl, S. |title=Erdős–Hajnal for graphs with no 5-hole |journal=[[Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society]] |date=2023 |volume=126 |issue=3 |pages=997–1014 |doi=10.1112/plms.12504| arxiv=2102.04994|s2cid=259380697|author1-link=Maria Chudnovsky }}</ref>
